extracted.intended_audience: US patent applicants and practitioners (including those filing PCT/foreign-priority national stage applications)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing the Abstract (Abstract of the Disclosure) section of a US utility patent application: content, required format and heading, forbidden wording, length/line limits, common pitfalls, and how to correct/amend abstracts for Paris/PCT priority filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the patent abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent abstract is a short section of a utility patent that concisely summarizes the invention. The purpose of the abstract is not to disclose all the details of the invention, but rather to provide a concise statement of the invention to enable readers to decide if they should read the patent specification for further details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the abstract focused on a short, high-level statement that lets readers decide whether to read the full specification; do not attempt full disclosure in the abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and heading of the abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferably located after the claims, the abstract should commence on a separate sheet under the heading “Abstract” or “Abstract of the Disclosure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the abstract on its own sheet and use the specified heading to conform with common US practice and examiner expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required narrative form and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract should be written in narrative form with clear and concise language (MPEP 608.01(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write in plain narrative sentences rather than lists of claim elements; emphasize clarity and brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid paraphrasing an independent claim
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a tendency to summarize the invention by simply paraphrasing an independent claim; such an approach can lead to an objectionable abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not merely restate claim language; provide a concise descriptive statement that is not simply a claim paraphrase (paraphrasing may be acceptable in the Brief Summary but not the abstract).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbidden phrases and words
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract should omit certain introductory or claim-like phrases and words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically avoid: "This disclosure concerns", "The disclosure defined by this invention", "This disclosure describes", and avoid claim-limiting or functional terms such as "means" and the archaic claim word "said". Also avoid phrasing that reads as boilerplate introductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not state merits, advantages, or compare to prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract should not refer to merits or advantages of the invention, or compare the invention to the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid promotional or comparative language in the abstract; keep it factual and descriptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and line limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract should contain no more than 150 words and 15 lines of text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft abstracts to be under 150 words (and under 15 lines) to comply with US practice; this is a common source of objections, especially for US applications claiming priority to foreign filings. If possible, draft foreign/PCT abstracts to be under 150 words to avoid later amendments or Preliminary Amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting abstracts for foreign and PCT applications
rubrics_metrics.description: When preparing abstracts in foreign or PCT applications, keep the abstract brief so it will comply with US practice when filing a US national stage or direct priority application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a practical matter, draft abstracts for foreign/PCT filings to be less than 150 words so you avoid a Preliminary Amendment or other corrections when entering the US national stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to correct or amend the abstract depending on filing path
rubrics_metrics.description: Correction procedures differ by filing route: if filing a new US application with a conventional Paris Convention priority claim, the abstract can be revised in the specification itself without showing markings; if entering the US national stage of a PCT application, a Preliminary Amendment with a marked-up version of the amended Abstract should be filed with the initial national stage filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be proactive: correct an over-long or objectionable abstract upon initial filing to avoid an unnecessary Office Action; use the appropriate amendment route (spec revision for new US filings with Paris priority vs Preliminary Amendment with marked-up abstract for PCT national stage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract is mandatory under US rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes, a patent abstract is required. 37 CFR 1.72 sets forth the requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the abstract as a mandatory part of the specification and ensure compliance with the cited regulation to avoid formal objections or Office Actions.
